summary: Describes the ODETTE File Transfer Protocol, designed for exchanging data files between trading partners, as in electronic data interchange. It comes from the European automotive industry community. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 5024.

eli5.summary: It is a set of rules for companies to send business files to each other reliably, like a special delivery service between factories and their suppliers.

subtitle: The file transfer protocol for electronic data interchange in the automotive supply chain.

tldr.problem: The European automotive industry needed a reliable, standard way to exchange business files between trading partners that works across different computer systems and networks.
tldr.mechanism: ODETTE-FTP defines a protocol where files are transferred through exchange buffers with negotiated parameters, speaker/listener roles, and confirmation mechanisms, originally over X.25 networks and later adapted for TCP/IP.
tldr.outcome: The protocol was widely deployed in European automotive supply networks, and RFC 5024 later consolidated and updated it, making it a standard approach for EDI that spans multiple locations and clearing centres.

today: RFC 2204 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 5024, which consolidates and updates the ODETTE-FTP specification for modern use.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2204 describes the ODETTE File Transfer Protocol (ODETTE-FTP), a protocol designed to exchange files between trading partners in electronic data interchange (EDI). The protocol emerged from the European automotive industry, developed by the Organisation for Data Exchange by Tele Transmission in Europe to facilitate reliable communication between factories, suppliers, and distribution centres.

The protocol was originally designed around the X.25 network standard but has been adapted to use TCP/IP for internet deployment. ODETTE-FTP is independent of the underlying system hardware and software, allowing computers of different sizes and manufacturers to communicate reliably. The protocol listens on TCP port 3305 and negotiates session parameters such as buffer sizes, transfer capabilities, and restart support during the initial connection.
sections.eli5: ODETTE-FTP is a set of rules for different computers to safely exchange business files with each other. It works even if the computers are different brands or sizes, and always confirms that files arrived correctly.

sections.title: Virtual Files and Attributes
sections.content:
ODETTE-FTP transfers data as Virtual Files, a standard representation that abstracts away differences between local file systems. Each Virtual File is identified by a dataset name, date stamp (YYMMDD), and time stamp (HHMMSS), which together uniquely identify the file assigned by bilateral agreement between trading partners. The Virtual File also specifies the originator and final destination of the data.

Virtual Files support four record formats: Fixed (all records same length), Variable (records can differ), Unstructured (raw data stream), and Text (ASCII with CR/LF line endings, max 2048 chars per line). The protocol negotiates a maximum record length and tracks file sizes in 1K (1024-byte) blocks. ODETTE-FTP can also restart interrupted transfers: fixed and variable format files restart on record boundaries, while unstructured and text files restart at 1K block offsets.
sections.eli5: A Virtual File is like a carefully labeled package: it has the name of the file, when it was made, who sent it, and where it needs to go. The protocol remembers how the data is organized so it can stop and restart without losing information.

sections.title: Session Phases and Message Exchange
sections.content:
An ODETTE-FTP session progresses through five phases. The Start Session Phase begins when one peer (the Initiator) connects to another (the Responder), which listens on port 3305. The Responder sends a ready message (SSRM), and both peers exchange Start Session (SSID) commands to negotiate protocol level, buffer sizes, compression support, restart capability, and a credit window (the number of data buffers the sender may transmit before waiting for acknowledgment).

The Start File Phase involves the Initiator (acting as Speaker) sending a Start File (SFID) command with the file name, timestamps, destination, originator, format, and record size. The Listener responds with acceptance (SFPA) or rejection (SFNA). If accepted, the Data Transfer Phase begins: the Speaker sends data buffers (DATA commands), and when the available credit is exhausted, must wait for a Credit (CDT) command from the Listener. The Speaker then sends an End File (EFID) command with the record count and unit count, and the Listener responds with acceptance (EFPA) or rejection (EFNA).

After each successful file transmission, the Speaker and Listener can exchange roles using the Change Direction (CD) command. Once all files are transmitted, the Speaker sends End Session (ESID) to terminate the session. Error conditions trigger an abort sequence instead of normal close.
sections.eli5: A session has clear steps: first the computers agree on how to talk (Start Session), then one says which file to send (Start File), data flows with pauses for breathing room (Data Transfer), and finally the sender says it is done (End File). They can then switch roles and send files the other way.

sections.title: Broadcast, Responses, and Clearing Centres
sections.content:
ODETTE-FTP supports advanced distribution patterns. A destination in the Start File command can specify either an explicit recipient or a group destination, allowing an intermediate location (such as a clearing centre) to broadcast a Virtual File to multiple destinations. The Listener rejects the file if the destination is unknown. This capability is essential in automotive supply networks where a single shipment notification might need to reach multiple suppliers or distribution points.

The protocol defines an End-to-End Response (EERP) command that notifies the originator of a Virtual File when it has been successfully delivered to its final destination. This allows the originator to perform housekeeping tasks such as deleting copies of delivered data. When a clearing centre broadcasts a file to multiple destinations, it must receive an EERP from all recipients before sending its own EERP to the upstream originator, ensuring complete delivery tracking across the supply chain. A Ready To Receive (RTR) command provides flow control for EERP messages, preventing congestion.

The protocol acknowledges that clearing centres may introduce processing errors unrelated to the protocol itself; such errors are a local responsibility and outside ODETTE-FTP's scope.
sections.eli5: Files can be sent to multiple places at once, like photocopying a memo to many desks. The protocol tracks confirmation all the way back to the sender, and lets them know when a file reaches its final destination so they can clean up their copies.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content:
ODETTE-FTP sends user identity and password information in clear text during the Start Session phase. The RFC explicitly recommends that implementors use a lower-layer security protocol to protect the session from identity collection. This reflects the protocol's 1980s origins, when security was often assumed to be handled by X.25 link-layer encryption or by operating in closed, controlled networks.

The protocol provides basic authentication through identification codes and passwords negotiated during session setup. Sessions use activity timers to detect hang conditions and include state machine validation to detect protocol errors. Error handling is split across layers: the protocol detects errors through its state machine and timers, while clearing centres and applications handle errors outside the protocol's scope.
sections.eli5: The protocol uses passwords, but sends them without hiding them. That is why it is recommended to use a secure tunnel or trusted network around it. The protocol also watches for computers that stop responding and catches messages that are out of order.
